Use any backend framework/language (Node.js, Express, Django, Spring Boot, Go, etc.) and any database (MongoDB, PostgreSQL, MySQL, Firebase, etc.).

Objective: Backend for a Secret Santa draw — everyone signs up, the system pairs each person to a giftee (never themselves), and each person can only ever see their own assignment.

Core Requirements:
- Auth: signup/login.
- Draw: once N people have joined, generate a valid pairing where no one is assigned to themselves.
- Private Reveal: /my-giftee returns only the caller's assignment — never the full list.

Bonus:
- Prevent mutual pairs (A→B and B→A) — optional.
- Lock the draw once it's run — no new joins after.
- Wishlist field per user, visible only to their assigned gifter.

Suggested Endpoints: POST /auth/signup, POST /auth/login, POST /auth/logout, POST /draw/run (admin), GET /participants (names only, no assignments), GET /participant/:id (own profile only), PATCH /participant/:id/wishlist, DELETE /participant/:id (admin, pre-draw only), GET /draw/status, POST /draw/lock (admin, manual close), GET /my-giftee (auth'd user), GET /my-wishlist-giver (reverse view — who's assigned to you, still private).

Deliverables: Source code (Git repository link); deployment link (optional); README & documentation (optional).
title: JC Task 1 — Secret Santa Assigner API

Objective: Single-elimination roast-battle tournament — contestants submit lines, the crowd votes per matchup, winners advance automatically.

Core Requirements:
- Register contestants + submit roast lines per round.
- Bracket generation for round 1, with bye handling for odd numbers.
- Time-boxed voting window: each matchup accepts votes only within a fixed duration after it opens (e.g. 5 min) — server-side enforced, not just frontend.
- Concurrency-safe tally: vote counts must update atomically — two votes landing at the same instant can't corrupt the count or let one user's request register twice.
- Auto-advance the winner the moment the window closes; handle ties (coin-flip or sudden-death re-vote).

Bonus:
- Email notification (Nodemailer or similar) to a contestant when they advance to the next round.
- /bracket/:tournamentId — full bracket view with the current round highlighted live.

Suggested Endpoints: POST /contestants, GET /contestants, DELETE /contestants/:id (pre-bracket only), POST /bracket/generate, GET /bracket/:tournamentId, POST /vote/:matchupId, GET /matchup/:id/status, GET /matchup/:id/results, POST /matchup/:id/tiebreak, POST /round/advance (system), GET /tournament/:id/winner, GET /contestant/:id/history.

Deliverables: Source code (Git repository link); deployment link (optional); README & documentation (optional).
title: SC Task 1 — Roast Battle Bracket API

Objective: Anonymous campus "rumors" that decay in credibility over time unless upvoted, with live updates.

Core Requirements:
- Post a rumor anonymously (category: academic/hostel/canteen/etc).
- Credibility score that decays with time, boosted by upvotes.
- Debunk: N flags auto-marks a rumor "debunked."
- Real-time feed (WebSockets): every connected client sees new rumors and live credibility/upvote changes pushed instantly — no polling.
- Anonymous session persistence: since there's no login, track each anonymous poster/voter via a session token so they can't upvote or flag the same rumor twice — and handle what happens if their session token is lost/refreshed mid-session (analogous to the "host leaves" edge case last year).

Bonus:
- /trending — top-N rumors by current decayed credibility, also pushed live.
- Rate-limit one new rumor per session per hour.

Suggested Endpoints: POST /session/init (anonymous token), GET /session/me, POST /rumor, GET /rumor/:id, GET /rumors (paginated/filtered), GET /rumor/category/:category, POST /rumor/:id/upvote, POST /rumor/:id/flag, GET /rumor/:id/credibility, PATCH /rumor/:id/debunk (system-triggered), GET /trending, WebSocket rumors/live.

Deliverables: Source code (Git repository link); deployment link (optional); README & documentation (optional).
title: SC Task 2 — Campus Rumor Mill API

prompt:
Objective: A streaming platform's recommender works for users with long watch histories but breaks for new users and new movies. Build a hybrid recommender that blends collaborative filtering with content features and leans on content as history thins out.

Dataset: MovieLens Latest Small (~100k ratings, 610 users, ~9,700 movies, ~1 MB) – https://files.grouplens.org/datasets/movielens/ml-latest-small.zip (no login needed; unzip into task2/data/. Optional larger run: https://files.grouplens.org/datasets/movielens/ml-1m.zip, which has genres but no tags.)
Note: every user has at least 20 ratings, so you must simulate new users yourself.

Base Requirements:
- Collaborative filtering: matrix factorization (SVD or ALS) as the base model. State your train/test split and why.
- Content model: use genres and tags (TF-IDF or embeddings) so movies with few or no ratings still get scores.
- Blend: content weight increases as a user's or movie's history shrinks. No fixed 50/50. Explain your weighting in 3-4 sentences.
- Cold-start test: for cold users, keep only their first 1-4 ratings in training and hold out the rest. Cold movies = fewer than 5 training ratings.
- Report Precision@10, Recall@10 and NDCG@10 for cold and warm slices in one table. RMSE alone is not accepted.
- Show 3 failure cases: what went wrong, why, and what might fix it.

Brownie Points:
- Compare against a pure popularity baseline and report the lift.
- Diversity or novelty re-ranking so the top 10 isn't only popular movies.
- Try text embeddings of tags or titles.

Deliverables: GitHub repo with README (setup, dependencies, how to reproduce results); analysis.ipynb (runs top to bottom without errors); 1-2 page write-up: approach, key decisions, results. Libraries: pandas, numpy, scipy, scikit-learn (scikit-surprise or implicit optional).
title: SC-AIML Task 3 — When the Recommender Has Nothing to Go On

prompt:
Objective: Build and audit a fraud detection system for an online payment platform, with a focus on determining whether the model and its evaluation can actually be trusted rather than simply maximizing accuracy.

Base Requirements:
- Explore the provided transaction dataset through EDA and identify important patterns, missing values, duplicates, outliers, class imbalance, and potentially suspicious features.
- Clean and preprocess the data by appropriately handling missing values, categorical variables, outliers, and other data-quality issues.
- Clearly justify the major preprocessing and feature-selection decisions.
- Train at least two suitable classification models, including a baseline model.
- Evaluate the models using appropriate metrics such as Precision, Recall, F1-score, ROC-AUC, and a Confusion Matrix.
- Explain why these metrics are more appropriate for fraud detection than relying only on accuracy.
- Audit the evaluation methodology for data leakage, overfitting, inappropriate features, and issues with the train-test split.
- Investigate whether a temporal train-test split would be more appropriate for the given dataset.

Brownie Points:
- Identify and demonstrate a potential data-leakage scenario.
- Compare random train-test splitting with a temporal split and analyze the difference in results.
- Identify features that may be suspicious, unrealistic, or unavailable at real-world prediction time.
- Test at least two robustness scenarios that could cause model performance to deteriorate.
- Analyze how class imbalance affects model performance.
- Tune or modify the model based on findings and demonstrate whether the change actually improves reliability.
- Perform detailed error analysis on false positives and false negatives.
- Compare model performance across different fraud/non-fraud thresholds.
- Discuss the trade-off between detecting fraud and incorrectly flagging legitimate transactions.

Deliverables: Google Colab notebook containing the complete EDA, preprocessing, modelling, evaluation, and model-audit pipeline; at least two trained classification models with their evaluation results; confusion matrices and relevant evaluation metrics; analysis of data leakage, overfitting, feature validity, and validation methodology; results from at least two robustness/failure scenarios; improved model with a comparison against the baseline; a concise final report explaining the major decisions, findings, and whether the model's reported performance can be trusted.
title: SC-AIML Task 4 — The Model You Shouldn't Trust

prompt:
Objective: A food-tech startup wants to rank Bangalore restaurants by Zomato rating. Use the data to show where "sort by rating" breaks, and recommend a better ranking signal.

Dataset: Zomato Bangalore Restaurants (~51k rows) – https://www.kaggle.com/himanshupoddar/zomato-bangalore-restaurants (download needs a free Kaggle login; put zomato.csv in your task1/ folder.)

Base Requirements:
- Clean the data: rate ("4.1/5", "NEW", "-"), approx_cost (commas), online_order, book_table, duplicates. Note each decision briefly.
- Find 2 patterns where "sort by rating" misleads. For each: show the numbers or a chart, and name the type of user who gets misled (e.g. a student wanting dinner under ₹200).
- Make 2 charts, each arguing one point, with a title, labelled axes, and a 2-4 sentence interpretation.
- Write memo.md (max 1 page) to the product team: your recommended ranking signal (what data, combined how), the 2 strongest reasons the naive approach fails, one thing you chose NOT to act on and why, and what extra data you'd want.

Brownie Points:
- A third pattern in the data.
- Compare a vote-weighted or Bayesian score against raw rating.
- Separate rankings by cost band or cuisine.
- Handle chain outlets and duplicate listings.

Deliverables: analysis.ipynb (runs top to bottom without errors) + memo.md; GitHub repo or Colab link. Libraries: pandas, numpy, matplotlib, seaborn.
title: Common Task 1 — Why Ratings Lie

prompt:
Objective: Build a small ML system that classifies student queries into categories such as academics, events, transport, clubs, facilities, or other.

Dataset: CLINC150 (general intent dataset, not campus-specific) – https://huggingface.co/datasets/DeepPavlov/clinc150

Base Requirements:
- Explain how you get to the six campus categories: map a set of CLINC150 intents, write your own queries (at least 10 per category), or both.
- Inspect and clean the text data, and train a classification model with a fixed random seed.
- Evaluate on a held-out test set using accuracy, precision, recall and F1-score.
- Provide a simple prediction interface through a notebook, CLI or small API.
- Show examples of correct and incorrect predictions.

Brownie Points:
- Compare two different models.
- Confusion matrix and error analysis.
- Confidence score for predictions.
- Handle an unknown/other class.
- Add a tiny web UI or API endpoint for live inference.

Deliverables: Source code; dataset or dataset-generation script; evaluation report; README with setup instructions and results.
title: AIML Task 2 — Campus Query Classifier

prompt:
Objective: Build an unsupervised ML pipeline that groups similar data points and evaluates the resulting clusters.

Dataset: UCI Iris – https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/53/iris

Base Requirements:
- Load and explore the dataset.
- Scale the numerical features where appropriate.
- Apply K-Means clustering.
- Use the Elbow Method and/or Silhouette Score to choose the number of clusters.
- Visualize and interpret the clusters.
- Compare the clusters with the original species labels only after clustering.

Brownie Points:
- Compare K-Means with DBSCAN.
- Use PCA for two-dimensional visualization.
- Analyse poorly separated samples.
- Compare results before and after scaling.

Deliverables: Notebook; dataset/source link; visualizations and evaluation results; short explanation of findings.
title: AIML Task 3 — Tabular Data Clustering

prompt:
Imagine you had to describe your favourite hobby using only visuals. How would you make someone understand what it feels like without explaining it to them?

Design a website experience that communicates your hobby primarily through visual storytelling, layout, colour, typography, imagery, and thoughtful UI/UX decisions.

Requirements:
- Choose any hobby you genuinely connect with.
- Your design should communicate the essence of the hobby without depending heavily on text.
- Focus on creating a clean, visually appealing, and intuitive user experience.
- Maintain a consistent visual language throughout the experience.
- Ensure the layout, hierarchy, navigation, spacing, typography, and overall flow are clear and purposeful.
- Create enough screens/sections to effectively communicate your concept and user journey.

Bonus:
- Add at least 1 meaningful interaction that contributes to the overall experience.
- Demonstrate how your design adapts to different screen sizes.
- Add animations or additional micro-interactions where they meaningfully enhance the experience.

AI is allowed. You may use AI tools for inspiration, ideation, visuals, coding, debugging, or other parts of the process. However, the core concept and design decisions must be your own. We want to see your thinking, not just what an AI tool can generate.

You do not need to complete the website fully. If your idea is ambitious, you may submit a partially completed prototype or implementation. What matters is how well you communicate your concept, demonstrate your design thinking, and create a clear and engaging user experience.

Submission: Figma prototype, along with a brief explanation of your concept and key design decisions.

We evaluate: Visual storytelling, creativity, UI quality, UX and usability, visual consistency, originality, and the thought behind your design decisions.

prompt:

title: Web Pentesting Automation Tool
prompt:
Develop an automated web penetration testing tool to identify SQL Injection, XSS, insecure cookie configurations, and missing security headers within a fictional corporate web environment.

Base Requirements: 1) Vulnerability Detection: Automated scanning for SQLi endpoints and XSS reflection points.
2) Configuration Audit: Validation of cookie attributes (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite) and critical security headers (CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options).
3) Targeting Logic: Ability to crawl or receive specific endpoints from the provided fictional company scenario.

Deliverables: 1) Source Code: A functional automation tool (Python, Go, or similar) implementing the detection logic.
2) Documentation: A brief 'How-to' guide for running the tool against the target scenario.
3) Pentest Report (Bonus): A structured summary detailing discovered vulnerabilities, severity levels, technical evidence, and remediation steps.

title: SSH Honeypot and Telemetry Processing
prompt:
Build an SSH honeypot to capture attacker interactions and analyze session telemetry for behavioral patterns and bot detection.

Base Requirements: 1) Logging: Record attacker IPs, timestamps, session summaries, and every executed command.
2) Payload Capture: Extract attempted URLs and malicious scripts/commands.
3) Telemetry Analysis: Produce insights on IP frequency, common commands, and distinguish between automated bots and human actors.

Deliverables: 1) Source Code: A functional SSH listener and log processing system.
2) Telemetry Report: A summary of malicious behavior patterns and IP analysis.
3) Visualizations (Bonus): Charts or graphs representing attack trends and threat metrics.
